an1.188:1.1: Koṇḍañña gained his nickname as he was the first person to realize the Dhamma after the Buddha ([sn56.11:14.3]()). His absence was due to his love of solitude, as expressed in his verses ([thag15.1:0.4]()). Due to this, he features rarely in the early texts, but the Buddha once saw him meditating ([ud7.6]()), and he once came to show extreme devotion to the Buddha ([sn8.9[()). | I try to supply key details from the Suttas and Vinaya for these “foremost individuals”. However, in several cases the individuals are unknown in early texts, in which case I utilize commentarial stories. For the full commentarial stories, see Malalasekera’s *Dictionary of Pali Proper Names*.
an1.189:1.1: Sāriputta, also called Upatissa, became a stream-enterer on hearing a short teaching from the monk Assaji ([pli-tv-kd1:23.5.6]()), whereupon he told his friend Moggallāna. They both promptly left their former teacher Sañjaya, a traumatic loss to Sañjaya and his community. [an4.172:2.1]() says that Sāriputta became enlightened a fortnight after he ordained, a detail confirmed in multiple parallels to this passage; [mn111:2.8]() details the practice he undertook in that fortnight. The Suttas feature his teachings extensively (eg. [thag17.2](), [snp4.16]()), but his detailed analytical style is best exemplified in such texts as [mn9](), [mn28](), and [mn140](). He is remembered in the tradition for his warmth and dignity of character. He passed away shortly before the Buddha ([sn47.13]()).
an1.190:1.1: Mahāmoggallāna (or simply Moggallāna; also called Kolita), displays his spectacular mastery of psychic powers in such texts as [mn37](), but also taught on the details of ethical conduct ([mn15]()), or conversed with Sāriputta on the motivations for misconduct ([mn5]()). After going forth with Sāriputta, he was advised by the Buddha on meditation ([an7.61]()). Like Sāriputta, he pre-deceased the Buddha ([sn47.14]()), but the circumstances of his death are not recorded and later accounts are not reliable. His verses are at [thag20.1]()).
an1.191:1.1: Mahākassapa was the former husband of Bhaddā Kāpilānī ([an1.244]()). He was known for his simple and austere lifestyle ([sn16.5]()), devotion to the Buddha ([sn16.11]()), support for the poor ([ud1.6]()), and love of nature ([thag18.2]()). He was the senior disciple to survive the Buddha ([dn16:6.19.1]()), and presided over the First Council ([pli-tv-kd21]()). His death is not recorded in early texts. Legend says he is still alive, meditating in a mountain cave where he awaits the next Buddha, to whom he will present his robe as an offering.
an1.192:1.1: Anuruddha was the brother of Ānanda and Mahānāma ([pli-tv-kd17:1.1.3]()) which, according to the commentary, makes the Buddha his cousin. He was an exponent of mindfulness meditation ([sn52.1](), etc.) and often practiced with his friends Nandiya and Kimbila ([mn31]()). His mastery of mind-reading is shown at the Buddha’s deathbed ([dn16:6.8.3]()). He mastered clairvoyance soon after going forth ([pli-tv-kd17:1.1.3](), and discussed related issues several times ([mn127]()). His verses are at [thag16.9]().
an1.193:1.1: Former ruler of the Sakyans ([pli-tv-kd17:1.3.1](), the luxury of his former life is emphasized in his appearances at [thag16.7]() and [ud2.10]().
an1.194:1.1: Bhaddiya’s enlightenment came when being taught by Sāriputta ([ud7.1]()), who, however, underestimated him and kept teaching anyway ([ud7.2]()). His verses are at [thag7.2](). He is praised by the Buddha at [sn21.6]() = [ud7.5]().
an1.195:1.1: Bhāradvāja the Alms-Gatherer declares enlightenment at [sn48.49](), for which he was praised as the foremost in roaring a lion’s roar. He was noted for his austere lifestyle ([ud4.6]()), which he explained in his verses at [thag2.2](), and touches on in his conversation on sense retraint with King Udena at [sn35.127](). He and Moggallāna once egged each other on to win a psychic power contest, for which he was reprimanded by the Buddha ([pli-tv-kd15:8.1.1]()).
an1.196:1.1: Puṇṇa son of Mantāṇī was most famous for his conversation with Sāriputta in [mn24](), on the strength of which he was said to be the best Dhamma speaker. His verse is at [thag1.4:1.7](). For his mother’s name, see note on [mn86:12.12]().
an1.197:1.1: Mahākaccāna was one of the great disciples, whose teachings specially emphasized the incisive analysis of consciousness through the lens of the six senses. His skill with detailed explanations of brief teachings  are on display at at [mn133](), [mn138](), and [an10.172](). Later he was to settle to the southwest in Avanti ([sn22.3]()), where he established the Dhamma in the region ([sn35.132]()).
